title: Performative Privacy: When Differential Privacy Maximizes Utility
content:
Computer Science > Machine Learning
  [Submitted on 28 Aug 2026]
    Title:Performative Privacy: When Differential Privacy Maximizes Utility
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Privacy-preserving learning is often motivated by the idea that protecting users' data can preserve trust and thus participation, improving utility in the long term. However, this claim has not been formalized so far. In parallel, performative learning provides a framework for studying learning systems whose deployment affects the data they later observe. In this work, we bring these two perspectives together and introduce \emph{performative privacy}, where data leakage reduces future participation. We study a simple model where agents repeatedly contribute data for mean estimation but may leave the system when their data is leaked. Privacy is implemented through differentially private mechanisms, creating a trade-off between estimation noise and future participation. We show, through a theoretical study of the dynamics and numerical experiments, that a finite privacy budget can outperform non-private estimation in the long term when the feedback loop between leakage and participation is sufficiently strong. This provides first evidence that differential privacy can be optimal not only as a protection mechanism, but also from the perspective of long-term utility.

report.summary: New research formalizes 'performative privacy,' showing finite differential privacy budgets can beat non-private learning long-term by preserving user participation.
report.background: Privacy-preserving machine learning has long assumed that protecting user data builds trust and keeps people engaged, but this intuition lacked formal proof. Meanwhile, performative learning studies how a model's deployment changes the data it later receives—a feedback loop. This paper merges these ideas. The authors model a scenario where users contribute data to estimate a mean, but may leave if their data is leaked. Differential privacy is applied to limit leakage, yet it adds noise to estimates. The key tension: more privacy means worse short-term estimates but better retention. By analyzing the resulting dynamics theoretically and numerically, they show that when the feedback from data leakage to participation is strong, a finite privacy budget can produce better long-term accuracy than no privacy at all. This is the first formal evidence that privacy can be an instrumentally optimal strategy for utility, not just a regulatory requirement.
key_points: The paper introduces 'performative privacy,' a framework that combines differential privacy with performative prediction to model how privacy choices influence future user participation. It treats privacy not as a static constraint but as a dynamic factor that shapes the data distribution the system will observe over time.

The authors use a simple mean-estimation setting where agents contribute data repeatedly and may exit if their data leaks. This isolates the core trade-off: stronger privacy reduces estimation accuracy via added noise, while weaker privacy risks losing participants and thus future data.

The main theoretical result shows that a finite privacy budget can outperform non-private estimation over the long run. This happens when the feedback loop between data leakage and user departure is sufficiently strong, meaning retention benefits outweigh noise costs.

Numerical experiments support the theoretical findings, demonstrating concrete dynamic trajectories where privacy-preserving mechanisms achieve lower long-term estimation error than non-private baselines. This validates that the effect is not merely an abstract possibility.

The work reframes differential privacy as a tool for long-term utility maximization. It suggests that privacy budgets should be chosen based on how sensitive user participation is to data leakage, not just on worst-case privacy guarantees alone.
report.impact: For AI developers, this research challenges the view that differential privacy is always a utility tax. Instead, privacy can be a strategic investment in data longevity, especially in consumer applications where trust drives retention. It motivates designing systems with explicit models of participation feedback, where privacy budgets are tuned to maximize sustained data quality rather than immediate accuracy. For the broader AI industry, it strengthens the business case for privacy-preserving techniques in federated learning, personalization, and user-generated data pipelines. Regular users benefit from a formal argument that privacy protections can improve, not degrade, the services they rely on—when deployed thoughtfully. The paper also opens new research directions in performative ML and adaptive privacy accounting.
report.tools: To explore differential privacy in practice, watch Opacus (PyTorch) and TensorFlow Privacy for training models with DP guarantees. Google's differential privacy library offers general-purpose mechanisms, while OpenMined's PyDP provides accessible Python implementations. For performative learning, check libraries like 'perfomative-prediction' or recent frameworks from Stanford's performative prediction group. These tools let practitioners experiment with privacy budgets and simulate feedback-driven data dynamics.
